title: Vietnam's S Shape: 1,650 km Long, Only 50 km Wide at the Waist

minor: 'More than 100 million people live along that thin line' suggests the population sits on the narrow waist. Most people live in the two deltas and coastal plains, so 'live along that long, thin country' would be safer.

'Your rice, your phone or your running shoes may well have travelled down it' is loose. Phone and footwear exports mostly leave via northern ports such as Hải Phòng, and Mekong rice leaves via Saigon-area ports, so little of it travels the length of the country. 'Leave through its ports' would be more accurate.
'a king took this very strip' is the Lý emperor Lý Thánh Tông. The word 'king' is loose, and the three districts lay in today's Quảng Bình and nearby, so 'around Đồng Hới' is approximate.
Laos was formally folded into the Indochinese Union in 1899. The 1893 treaty with Siam is the date it came under French control, so 'added after a treaty in 1893' is acceptable but compressed.
The 1999 China-Vietnam land border treaty was signed on 30 December 1999 and entered into force in 2000. 'A new treaty in 1999' is fine.
'A 2017 paper by the same group' means the same lead author and team (Minderhoud et al.), not identical authorship.
The July 2025 tariff was 20 percent, with a separate 40 percent rate on transshipped goods. Stating the 20 percent alone is not wrong.
'A thousand years ago the Vietnamese state held only the northern basket' is a round figure and fits the period around the early 11th century.

shots.vo: So why is Vietnam shaped like an S, and why so thin in the middle?
The answer starts in 1069, when a king took this very strip of land.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange: a medieval army column with banners crossing a narrow coastal plain below forested mountains, figures small and distant, no faces in close-up, no text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Vietnam sits on the eastern rim of Indochina, with China to the north and Laos and Cambodia to the west.
The thinnest stretch lies near the city of Đồng Hới, where the Lao border runs closest to the sea.
At that waist the country is more than thirty times longer than it is wide.
Its land borders run about 4,600 kilometres, and the longest, some 2,160 kilometres, is with Laos.
The coastline is shorter, yet even here the figures differ, depending on how it is counted.

map.label: The coast, Móng Cái to Hà Tiên

shots.vo: Vietnam's government counts 3,260 kilometres of mainland coast, while the CIA World Factbook lists 3,444 kilometres.
The thin waist follows a wall of mountains, the Annamite Range, which Vietnamese call Trường Sơn.
It runs roughly 1,100 kilometres down the west, and for long stretches the border with Laos follows its heights.
Between those heights and the sea, the centre is a chain of narrow coastal plains cut by short, steep rivers.
Vietnamese often picture their country as a carrying pole, with a basket of rice hanging from each end.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange: a bamboo carrying pole resting on a shoulder seen from behind, two heavy baskets of rice at each end, a paddy field beyond, no face, no text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: The northern basket is the Red River Delta, about 15,000 square kilometres of farmland around Hanoi, the capital.
The southern basket is the Mekong Delta, about 40,000 square kilometres spreading south-west of Ho Chi Minh City.
The Mekong Delta harvested about 24 million tonnes of rice in 2023, more than half of the national crop.

stat.label: Rice harvested in the Mekong Delta, 2023 (GSO)

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: flat delta rice fields at harvest cut by straight canals to the horizon, small wooden boats loaded with sacks, top third plain dark sky, no faces, no text

shots.vo: Much of it is sold abroad, and in 2024 rice exports reached a record of about nine million tonnes.

chart.title: A record harvest abroad
chart.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam / Vietnam Customs

shots.vo: Linking the baskets are one main road, National Route 1, and one railway, finished by the French in 1936.
That line is about 1,726 kilometres long, and even the fastest passenger trains take more than 30 hours.
And the slim waist around Đồng Hới is where Vietnam has been cut in two, and not only once.
Before the next part, one thing: episodes like this take real work, and subscribing is free.

shots.vo: A thousand years ago, the Vietnamese state held only the northern basket, the Red River Delta and its hills.
Chinese dynasties had ruled that delta for most of the thousand years since the Han conquest of 111 BCE.
In 938, at the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River, the commander Ngô Quyền defeated a Southern Han fleet.
His men had driven iron-tipped stakes into the riverbed, hidden by the high tide, and waited for it to fall.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange: a wide river estuary at low tide, rows of tall wooden stakes rising from the mud, distant wooden ships with sails, figures small, no faces, no text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Independence followed, and the northern line was later fixed by a Sino-French convention in 1887 and a new treaty in 1999.
To the south lay Champa, a chain of kingdoms along the central coast, with its own ports, temples and script.
Its brick temples still stand at Mỹ Sơn, near Đà Nẵng, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.
shots.prompt: Ancient Cham red-brick temple towers with weathered carved walls, partly overgrown, standing in a jungle valley ringed by green hills near Mỹ Sơn, Vietnam, soft morning light, wide documentary photo, no people, no text, no logos, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: In 1069 the Lý dynasty took three Cham districts, the land around today's Đồng Hới, right at the narrow waist.

map.label: Three districts move north to south

shots.vo: In 1306 a royal marriage moved the line again, as two districts around Huế were exchanged for Princess Huyền Trân.
In 1471 the armies of Emperor Lê Thánh Tông took the Cham capital of Vijaya, near today's Quy Nhơn.
Vietnamese historians call this long push the Nam tiến, the southward advance, and it ran for more than seven centuries.
From 1627 the Trịnh lords of the north and the Nguyễn lords of the south fought seven campaigns over the country.
The Nguyễn held the line behind long earthen walls near Đồng Hới, built straight across the narrowest part of the map.
After 1672 the fighting stopped at the Gianh River, which served as a border for roughly a hundred years.
Behind that line the Nguyễn kept moving south, into lands around the Mekong mouths that the Khmer kingdom had held.
In 1698 the commander Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh set up a Vietnamese administration at Gia Định, the town that became Saigon.
Cambodians still call the delta Kampuchea Krom, lower Cambodia, and Saigon's old Khmer name was Prey Nokor.

map.label: Kampuchea Krom (Khmer name for the delta)

shots.vo: In 1832 Emperor Minh Mạng abolished the last Cham principality, around Phan Rang, and the S was nearly complete.
The country now ran from the Chinese hills to the Gulf of Thailand, held together by one narrow coastal thread.
Then France arrived, taking southern provinces by treaty in 1862 and 1867, and making the rest a protectorate in 1884.
In 1887 Paris grouped its colonies as French Indochina, and Laos was added after a treaty with Siam in 1893.
Inside that union, the lines between Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia were drawn as internal French administrative boundaries.
In July 1954 the Geneva Accords split the country again, at a provisional line near the 17th parallel.

document.title: Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities in Viet-Nam, Geneva, 20 July 1954
document.highlight: A provisional military demarcation line shall be fixed, on either side of which the forces of the two parties shall be regrouped after their withdrawal

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: a long conference table under tall windows with stacked papers and pens, empty chairs, top third plain dark wall, no faces, no readable text

shots.vo: That line followed the Bến Hải River, with a demilitarised zone up to five kilometres deep on either side.
It ran about 70 kilometres south of Đồng Hới, once more across the narrow middle of the S.
Wartime supply routes ran west through Laos and Cambodia, along the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
The country was formally reunified in July 1976, and the line on the Bến Hải vanished from the map.
But the S does not stop at the beach, and the lines being drawn now are out at sea.
Vietnam's whole eastern side faces one sea, the South China Sea on most maps and the East Sea in Vietnam.

map.label: South China Sea (East Sea in Vietnam)

shots.vo: Under the 1982 UN law of the sea, a coast can claim an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles.
Off this long coast, Vietnam's zone meets rival claims, above all the dashed line China draws around most of the sea.
China has held the Paracel Islands, east of Đà Nẵng, since January 1974, and Vietnam and Taiwan also claim them.

map.label: Paracels: held by China since 1974, claimed by Vietnam and Taiwan (disputed)

shots.vo: Further south, China, Taiwan and Vietnam each claim all the Spratlys, while the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei claim parts.
Vietnam holds more Spratly features than any other claimant, according to the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at CSIS.
In recent years both China and Vietnam have enlarged reefs with dredged sand, adding harbours, buildings and runways.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange: a low coral reef in open ocean with a dredger pumping sand, a straight new runway and harbour basin taking shape, seen from high above, no people visible, no text, no flags, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: In 2016 a tribunal, in a case brought by the Philippines, rejected China's claim to historic rights inside the line.

document.title: Permanent Court of Arbitration, South China Sea Arbitration, Award of 12 July 2016
document.highlight: there was no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources within the sea areas falling within the 'nine-dash line'

shots.prompt: A map of the South China Sea with China's dashed line drawn around most of the sea; the dashed line is highlighted and a tribunal stamp marked 'historic rights rejected' is placed on the area inside it.

shots.vo: Beijing rejected the award the same day, calling it null and void, with no binding force.

quote.text: The award is null and void and has no binding force. China neither accepts nor recognizes it.
quote.who: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of China

shots.vo: China's case at its strongest is history: it says Chinese sailors named and used these islands long before modern sea law.
A Chinese government map first drew a dashed line around the sea in the late 1940s, long before 1982.
Vietnam answers with its own archives, citing Nguyễn-era records of royal crews sent to the Paracels.

map.label: Vietnam's claim: Nguyễn records and UNCLOS (disputed)

shots.vo: So which should weigh more on this map, the older records or the newer law?
In May 2014 China placed an oil rig near the Paracels, in waters Vietnam claims, and it stayed ten weeks.

headline.text: Chinese oil rig set up in waters near the Paracels that Vietnam claims

shots.prompt: A map of the Paracel Islands showing an oil rig marker inside Vietnam's claimed zone, labelled May 2014, then the marker pulled away and labelled 'withdrawn July'.

shots.vo: Vietnam's 2019 defence white paper sets out four noes, among them no military alliances and no foreign bases.

document.title: 2019 Viet Nam National Defence, Ministry of National Defence, November 2019
document.highlight: No military alliances; no siding with one country against another; no foreign military bases; no using force or threatening to use force

shots.vo: Its trade leans both ways too: in 2024 its biggest supplier was China and its biggest customer the United States.
The two governments even count that trade differently, and the gap between their figures is wide.
The US Census Bureau puts the 2024 goods gap at 123.5 billion dollars, Vietnam's statistics office at 104.6 billion.
The other pressure comes down the Mekong, which passes China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand and Cambodia before reaching Vietnam.
China has built 11 dams on the river's upper main stem, according to the Stimson Center's Mekong Dam Monitor.
Critics downstream say the dams trap water and sediment; China says they release water in dry seasons and ease floods.
In August 2024 Cambodia broke ground on the Funan Techo canal, some 180 kilometres from Phnom Penh to Kep.
Vietnam has asked for data on its effect; Cambodia says the canal draws little water and is its sovereign project.
And beneath all of this, the southern basket itself is sinking.
A 2019 study in Nature Communications found the Mekong Delta stands on average just 0.8 metres above sea level.

stat.label: Average height of the Mekong Delta above sea level (Minderhoud et al., 2019)

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: a flat delta landscape where a river bank sits barely above the water line, stilt houses and palms, top third plain dark sky, no faces, no text

shots.vo: A 2017 paper by the same group ties much of the sinking to groundwater pumping, lowering parts of the delta a centimetre or more yearly.

map.label: Subsidence ≥1 cm a year in parts

shots.vo: In the dry seasons of 2016 and 2020, salt water pushed far up the delta's rivers and into its rice fields.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and muted orange: cracked dry rice paddies beside a wide brackish canal under a pale hazy sky, an empty wooden boat on the bank, no people, no text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: If that continues, the southern basket could lose farmland at its edges, thinning the broad end of the S.
So what happens to a country shaped like a carrying pole when one of its baskets begins to tip?
The second scenario runs the other way: in November 2024 the National Assembly approved a high-speed line along the S.

document.title: National Assembly of Vietnam, Resolution 172/2024/QH15, 30 November 2024
document.highlight: Investment policy for the high-speed railway on the North–South axis

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: a large assembly hall seen from the back gallery, rows of empty seats and a distant podium, top third plain dark ceiling, no faces, no readable text

shots.vo: The planned line runs 1,541 kilometres, Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City, for trains of up to 350 kilometres an hour.
Its estimated cost is about 67 billion dollars, with completion targeted for 2035.

stat.label: Estimated cost of the North–South high-speed railway (Resolution 172/2024/QH15)

shots.prompt: Duotone plate, dark slate and muted orange: an unfinished concrete railway viaduct marching across rice fields toward distant hills, cranes on the skyline, top third plain dark sky, no people, no text

shots.vo: If it is built, the two baskets would be much closer by rail than the 30-plus hours today.
Supporters say it would tie the narrow middle to both ends; critics have asked whether its cost can be repaid.

shots.vo: Which brings us back to the waist at Đồng Hới, and to what the S really is.
In one reading, the S is less a coastline than a route that the state and settlers followed south between mountains and sea.
Next, another country squeezed between mountains and an ocean: Chile, about 4,300 kilometres long and on average 177 kilometres wide.
